source.excerpt: You can't teach an old dogma new tricks.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ records that the saying was ascribed to Parker in The Algonquin Wits (1968), edited by Robert E. Drennan, listed among her witticisms “without any additional context”. QI notes the citation as verified on paper: Citadel Press, New York, quote page 124.

That is a year after Parker died, and QI says so directly: “Parker died in 1967, and it would be nice to have an earlier linkage. Perhaps future research will discover a better citation for her.” No primary source in her own hand or voice has been found, which is why this page says attributed rather than verified.

She did not coin it. QI’s earliest instance is a 3 May 1928 Life magazine parody section ↗, in a piece about the film star Clara Bow, using the affirmative form: “She has proved that you can teach an old dogma new tricks!” QI traces further instances in 1929, 1933 and 1943, and suggests the pun “may have been independently concocted on multiple occasions”.

Our two anchor sources disagree on the verdict, and we are following the specialist. Wikiquote files the line under Misattributed ↗, citing an anonymous 1953 instance in the trade journal Sales Management. QI, which examined the question at length, concludes instead that Parker “probably did employ” the 1968 version though the evidence “is not decisive”. Both agree she was not the originator; they differ on whether she ever said it.
source.excerptNote: The line as printed in Drennan’s 1968 collection, which Quote Investigator verified on paper ↗ at quote page 124. The 1928 antecedent runs the other way: “She has proved that you can teach an old dogma new tricks!”

source.rightsNote: This exact wording is first documented in The Algonquin Wits (1968), so it is treated as in copyright in the United States. The 1928 Life antecedent is old enough to be public domain, but it is a different sentence — the affirmative form, about Clara Bow — and public-domain status does not carry across to the negative version quoted here. author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.heading: About Dorothy Parker
author.metaLine: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and short-story writer
author.bio: Dorothy Parker (born Dorothy Rothschild, 22 August 1893 — 7 June 1967) was an American poet, critic, short-story writer and screenwriter, and a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table. Her collections include Enough Rope (1926) and Death and Taxes (1931). Her particular gift was compression — the review or riposte that lands in a single line — which is both why this pun sits so naturally under her name and why so many unsourced ones end up there too.

misattribution.heading: What she is wrongly given credit for
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is not the problem — Quote Investigator thinks Parker probably did say it. What is wrong is the assumption that she made it up.

items.scope: The claim that she coined it
items.why: The pun was already in print in a 3 May 1928 Life magazine parody ↗, in the affirmative form, and recurs in 1929, 1933 and 1943. QI calls it “unlikely that she crafted it” and suggests it may have been invented independently more than once.

Wikiquote lists the line under Misattributed ↗, pointing to an anonymous 1953 instance in Sales Management. We follow Quote Investigator’s fuller treatment instead, but readers should know the two sources reach different verdicts.

misattribution.truthLine: Credibly Parker’s to have said, but not hers to have invented — see Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗, which runs from 1928 to 1986.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: A pun this economical — one letter added to a proverb everyone already knows — is almost designed to be reinvented. That is exactly what Quote Investigator’s chronology shows: a 1928 magazine parody, a 1933 column about the end of Prohibition, a 1943 economics address, a 1973 book review, and Tom Lehrer’s Vatican Rag along the way. No single line of descent connects them.

It is also why the attribution question here is milder than usual. Parker is not being credited with someone else’s sentence so much as with a joke that was in the air, and the honest answer is a divided one: she may well have said it, and she certainly did not invent it.
detailsBody: This page is the rare case where our two anchor sources disagree, and we have kept the disagreement visible rather than picking the tidier answer. Wikiquote files the line as misattributed on the strength of a 1953 anonymous instance. Quote Investigator, working from a longer chronology that reaches back to 1928, concludes Parker probably did use the version Drennan printed. Both findings rest on real citations; they answer slightly different questions, and only one of them — did she originate it? — has a firm answer, which is no.
context.pull: She may well have said it. She certainly did not invent it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator records the saying ascribed to Dorothy Parker in The Algonquin Wits (1968), ed. Robert E. Drennan, Citadel Press, quote page 124, verified on paper, and notes Parker died in 1967.

Quote Investigator gives the earliest instance as a 3 May 1928 Life magazine parody section about Clara Bow using the affirmative form "She has proved that you can teach an old dogma new tricks!", and concludes Parker probably did employ the 1968 version though the evidence is not decisive and it is unlikely she crafted it.
Wikiquote files "You can't teach an old dogma new tricks." under Misattributed on its Dorothy Parker page, citing Drennan 1968 p. 124 and an anonymous 1953 instance in Sales Management vol. 70 p. 80.

Wikipedia gives Dorothy Parker as born Dorothy Rothschild, 22 August 1893, died 7 June 1967, poet, critic and screenwriter, founding member of the Algonquin Round Table, with collections Enough Rope (1926) and Death and Taxes (1931).
The Internet Archive holds a Citadel Press edition of The Algonquin Wits.
